column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 27: “Righteousness is good character”

column2: From al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Righteousness is good character, and sin is what wavers in your soul and you dislike people coming to know of it.” Muslim reported it.
From Wābiṣah ibn Maʿbad, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: “You have come to ask about righteousness and sin?”

I said: Yes. He said: “Consult your heart. Righteousness is that with which the soul is at ease and with which the heart is at ease; and sin is what wavers in the soul and moves to and fro in the breast, even if people give you a ruling, and give you rulings again.”
The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: A ḥasan hadith, which we have narrated in the Musnads of the two imams Aḥmad and al-Dārimī with a ḥasan chain.

As for the hadith of al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, Muslim recorded it through the narration of Muʿāwiyah ibn Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father, from al-Nawwās. Muʿāwiyah, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and his father are narrators whose hadith Muslim alone recorded, not al-Bukhārī.
As for the hadith of Wābiṣah, Imam Aḥmad recorded it by way of Ḥammād ibn Salamah, from al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Salām, from Ayyūb ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn Mikraz, from Wābiṣah ibn Maʿbad, who said:
I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intending to leave nothing of righteousness and sin without asking about it, and he said to me:
“Come near, Wābiṣah.” So I came near him until my knee touched his knee, and he said: “Wābiṣah, shall I tell you what you have come to ask about, or will you ask me?”

I said: Messenger of Allah, tell me. He said: “You have come to ask me about righteousness and sin.” I said: Yes. He gathered his three fingers together and began tapping my chest with them, saying: “Wābiṣah, consult your soul. Righteousness is that with which the heart is at ease and the soul is at ease; and sin is
what wavers in the heart and moves to and fro in the breast, even if people give you a ruling, and give you rulings again.”

In another narration of Imam Aḥmad's, al-Zubayr did not hear it from Ayyūb; he said: His companions who sat with him told me, and I had seen him. So there are two things in the chain of this hadith, each of which makes it weak.
The first is the break between al-Zubayr and Ayyūb,
for he narrated it from people he did not name.

All three editions (al-Faḥl, Arnaʾūṭ, Abū al-Nūr) print «لم يسمعهم» (“whom he did not hear”), which contradicts al-Zubayr's own statement just quoted that these people told him. It is read as «لم يسمّهم» (“whom he did not name”), which gives the break described.

The second is the weakness of this al-Zubayr. Al-Dāraquṭnī said: He narrated objectionable (munkar) hadiths. Ibn Ḥibbān also declared him weak, but he called him Ayyūb ibn ʿAbd al-Salām and so got his name wrong. There is another route from Wābiṣah, which Imam Aḥmad also recorded, through the narration of Muʿāwiyah ibn Ṣāliḥ,

from Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Sulamī, who said: I heard Wābiṣah — and he related the hadith in brief. Its wording is: He said: “Righteousness is that to which your breast opens, and sin is what wavers in your breast, even if people give you a ruling about it.”
As for this al-Sulamī, ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: He is unknown.

Al-Bazzār and al-Ṭabarānī recorded it, and in their versions he is Abū ʿAbdillāh al-Asadī. Al-Bazzār said: We do not know anyone who has named him. So he said; but in some narrations he is named Muḥammad.

The ḥāfiẓ ʿAbd al-Ghanī ibn Saʿīd said: If someone were to say that he is Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd al-Maṣlūb, I would not dispute it. This al-Maṣlūb (“the Crucified”) was crucified by al-Manṣūr for heresy (zandaqah), and he is notorious for lying and fabrication; but he did not live to meet Wābiṣah. And Allah knows best.
This hadith has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ by many routes, some of which are sound. Imam Aḥmad recorded it,
as did Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, by way of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, from Zayd ibn Sallām, from his grandfather Mamṭūr, from Abū Umāmah, who said: A man said:
Messenger of Allah, what is sin?

He said: “When something wavers in your breast, leave it.” This is a sound chain meeting Muslim's conditions, for he recorded the hadith of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr from Zayd ibn Sallām, and Aḥmad affirmed that Yaḥyā heard from him, though Ibn Maʿīn denied it.

Imam Aḥmad recorded, through the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zabr: I heard Muslim ibn Mishkam say: I heard Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī say: I said: Messenger of Allah, tell me what is lawful for me and what is forbidden to me. He said: “Righteousness is that in which the soul finds rest

and with which the heart is at ease; and sin is that in which the soul does not find rest and with which the heart is not at ease, even if those who give rulings give you a ruling.” This too is a sound chain. ʿAbdullāh ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zabr is a well-known trustworthy narrator whom al-Bukhārī recorded, and Muslim ibn Mishkam is also a well-known trustworthy narrator.

Al-Ṭabarānī and others recorded, with a weak chain, from the hadith of Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ, who said: I said to the Prophet ﷺ: Give me a ruling on a matter about which I will ask no one after you. He said: “Consult your soul.” I said: How am I to do that?
He said: “Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt, even if those who give rulings give you a ruling.” I said: And how am I to do that?
He said: “Place your hand on your heart, for the heart finds rest in what is lawful and does not find rest in what is unlawful.”
Something similar is narrated from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, also with a weak chain.

Ibn Lahīʿah reported, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb, that Suwayd ibn Qays told him, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muʿāwiyah, that a man asked the Prophet ﷺ: Messenger of Allah, what is lawful for me, as against what is unlawful for me?
He repeated it to him three times, and each time the Prophet ﷺ was silent. Then he said: “Where is the questioner?”
He said: Here I am, Messenger of Allah. And, gesturing with his fingers, he said: “Whatever your heart rejects, leave it.”
Abū al-Qāsim al-Baghawī recorded it in his Muʿjam, and said: I do not know whether ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muʿāwiyah heard from the Prophet ﷺ or not,
and I know no hadith of his besides this one.
I say: He is ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥudayj, whose lineage is given in Ibn al-Mubārak's Kitāb al-Zuhd. This ʿAbd al-Raḥmān is a well-known Successor, so his hadith is mursal.
It is authentically reported that Ibn Masʿūd said: Sin is what pricks the hearts (ḥawāzz al-qulūb). Imam Aḥmad cited it as evidence, and reported it from Jarīr, from Manṣūr,
from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his father, who said: ʿAbdullāh said: Beware of what pricks the hearts (ḥazzāz al-qulūb); whatever pricks at your heart, leave it.
Abū al-Dardāʾ said: Good lies in tranquillity, and evil in doubt.
It is narrated from Ibn Masʿūd, by a broken route, that he was asked: What do you say of something that wavers in our breasts, when we do not know whether it is lawful or unlawful?

He said: Beware of the things that scratch (al-ḥakkākāt), for they are sin. Ḥazz (pricking) and ḥakk (scratching) are close in meaning; what is meant is whatever leaves in the heart a sense of tightness and constraint, aversion and dislike.

These hadiths, then, contain an explanation of righteousness and sin, and some of them an explanation of the lawful and the unlawful. In the hadith of al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān the Prophet ﷺ explained righteousness as good character,
while in the hadith of Wābiṣah and others he explained it as that with which the heart and the soul are at ease, just as he explained the lawful in the same way in the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah.
His explanation of righteousness differed only
because righteousness is used in two specific senses.

The first concerns dealing with people by treating them with kindness. It is sometimes applied specifically to kindness to parents, as in the phrase “righteousness towards parents” (birr al-wālidayn), but it is often applied to kindness to people in general. Ibn al-Mubārak compiled a book he named Kitāb al-Birr wa-l-Ṣilah (“The Book of Righteousness and Keeping Ties”),

and Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī likewise have a Book of Righteousness and Keeping Ties. Such a book covers kindness to people in general, and righteousness towards parents is put first in it, ahead of others.
In the hadith of Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather: He said: Messenger of Allah, to whom should I be dutiful?
He said: “Your mother.” He said: Then whom?
He said: “Then your father.” He said: Then whom?
He said: “Then the nearest, and then the next nearest.”
Of this meaning is the Prophet's saying ﷺ: “An accepted (mabrūr) Ḥajj has no reward but Paradise.”
In the Musnad, he ﷺ was asked about the righteousness (birr) of Ḥajj, and he said: “Feeding people and spreading the greeting of peace”; in another narration: “and good speech.”
Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) used to say: Righteousness is an easy thing: a cheerful face and gentle speech.

When righteousness is paired with taqwā, as in His words, the Mighty and Majestic, “Help one another in righteousness and taqwā” [al-Māʾidah 5:2], righteousness may mean dealing with people with kindness, and taqwā dealing with Allah, the Real (al-Ḥaqq), by obeying Him

and avoiding what He has forbidden. Or righteousness may mean doing the obligatory duties, and taqwā avoiding the forbidden things. In His words, Exalted is He, “And do not help one another in sin and aggression” [al-Māʾidah 5:2], sin may mean acts of disobedience, and aggression wronging people;
or sin may mean what is forbidden in itself, such as fornication, theft and drinking wine, and aggression going beyond what is permitted into what is prohibited, in matters whose kind is permitted:

such as killing, along with one whose killing is permitted in retaliation, someone whose killing is not; taking more than is due from people in zakāh and the like; exceeding the number of lashes commanded in the prescribed punishments; and so on.
The second sense of righteousness is that it means doing all acts of obedience, outward and inward, as in His words, Exalted is He:

“But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets; who gives wealth, despite his love of it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer and those who ask, and for freeing slaves; who keeps up the prayer and gives zakāh; and those who keep their covenants when they make them, and the patient in poverty, hardship and the heat of battle. It is they who are truthful, and it is they who are the God-fearing” [al-Baqarah 2:177].
It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about faith and recited this verse.

Righteousness in this sense includes all the inward acts of obedience, such as faith in Allah, His angels, His Books and His messengers, and the outward acts of obedience, such as spending wealth on what Allah loves, keeping up the prayer, giving zakāh, fulfilling covenants, and patience: with what is decreed, such as illness and poverty, and in acts of obedience, such as patience when meeting the enemy.
The Prophet's answer ﷺ in the hadith of al-Nawwās may include all of these traits,

because good character may mean taking on the character of the Sharīʿah and adopting the manners in which Allah has trained His servants in His Book, as the Exalted said to His Messenger ﷺ: “And indeed you are of a great character” [al-Qalam 68:4].

ʿĀʾishah said: His character ﷺ was the Qurʾān. She meant that he took on its manners, doing what it commands and avoiding what it forbids, so that acting on the Qurʾān became his character, like an innate disposition and nature that never left him. This is the best, noblest and most beautiful of characters.
It has been said that the whole of the religion is character.

In the hadith of Wābiṣah he said: “Righteousness is that with which the heart is at ease and with which the soul is at ease”; in one narration: “that to which the breast opens.” He explained the lawful in a similar way, as in the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah and others.

This shows that Allah created His servants with an innate disposition to know the truth, to find rest in it and to accept it, and that He implanted in their natures a love of that and an aversion to its opposite.

This may be included in His words, in the hadith of ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār: “I created My servants upright (ḥunafāʾ), Muslims; then the devils came to them and led them away from their religion, made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them to associate with Me that for which I had sent down no authority.”

And in his words: “Every child is born upon the natural disposition (fiṭrah); then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a whole animal: do you find any among them with its ears cut off?”
Abū Hurayrah said: Recite, if you wish: “The natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no altering Allah's creation” [al-Rūm 30:30].

For this reason Allah called what He commanded maʿrūf, the known, and what He forbade munkar, the rejected. He said: “Indeed, Allah commands justice, excellence and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing (munkar) and transgression” [al-Naḥl 16:90]; and describing the Messenger ﷺ, He said:

“He makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the foul things” [al-Aʿrāf 7:157]. He also told that the hearts of the believers find rest in His remembrance. So the heart which the light of faith has entered, and which has been opened and expanded by it, finds rest in the truth, is at ease with it and accepts it, and recoils from falsehood, dislikes it and does not accept it.

Muʿādh ibn Jabal said: I warn you against the slip of the wise man, for Satan may utter a word of misguidance on the tongue of the wise man, and the hypocrite may utter a word of truth. Muʿādh was asked: How am I to know that the wise man may utter a word of misguidance and that the hypocrite may utter a word of truth?
He said: Avoid, in the speech of the wise man, the glaring statements of which people say: What is this?
But do not let that turn you away from him, for perhaps he will go back on it; and take the truth when you hear it, for there is a light upon the truth. Abū Dāwūd recorded it.
In a narration of his, he said: Rather, [avoid] whatever in the wise man's words is unclear to you, so that you say: What did he mean by this word?
This shows that truth and falsehood are not confused for the discerning believer. Rather, he recognises the truth by the light upon it, so that his heart accepts it, and he recoils from falsehood,
rejecting it and not recognising it. Of this meaning is the Prophet's saying ﷺ: “At the end of time there will be people who tell you things that neither you nor your forefathers have heard,
so beware of them.” That is, they will bring what the hearts of the believers reject and do not recognise. And in his words,

“neither you nor your forefathers”, there is an indication that whatever has become settled as known among the believers over long ages and the passing of time is the truth, and that whatever objectionable thing has been introduced after that has no good in it.

So the hadith of Wābiṣah, and those like it in meaning, show that one should turn to the heart when things are unclear: whatever the heart finds rest in and the breast opens to is righteousness and lawful, and whatever is otherwise is sin and unlawful.

His words in the hadith of al-Nawwās, “Sin is what wavers in the breast and you dislike people coming to know of it,” indicate that sin is whatever leaves in the breast a sense of constraint, tightness, disquiet and agitation,

so that the breast does not open to it; and that, besides this, it is objectionable to people, so that they would reject it if they came to know of it. This is the highest level of recognising sin when things are unclear: it is what people find objectionable, the one who does it and others alike.
Of this meaning is Ibn Masʿūd's saying: Whatever the believers see as good is good with Allah, and whatever the believers see as bad is bad with Allah.

His words in the hadiths of Wābiṣah and Abū Thaʿlabah, “even if those who give rulings give you a ruling,” mean that whatever wavers in a person's breast is sin, even if someone else gives him a ruling that it is not sin.

This is a second level: the thing is objectionable to the one who does it but not to others, and he has made this sin too. But this is only so when the person is one whose breast has been opened by faith,

and the one giving the ruling gives it merely on conjecture or out of an inclination towards desire, without evidence from the Sharīʿah. Where the one giving the ruling has evidence from the Sharīʿah for it, the one seeking the ruling must defer to it,

even if his breast does not open to it. This is like the concessions of the Sharīʿah, such as breaking the fast when travelling or ill, shortening the prayer when travelling, and the like, to which the breasts of many ignorant people do not open; that counts for nothing.

The Prophet ﷺ sometimes commanded his Companions to do things to which the breasts of some of them did not open, so that they held back from doing them, and he was angered by that. So it was when he commanded them to change their Ḥajj into an ʿUmrah,

and those of them who disliked it disliked it; and when he commanded them to slaughter their sacrificial animals and come out of iḥrām at the ʿUmrah of al-Ḥudaybiyah, and they disliked it, and disliked his agreement with Quraysh that he would go back that year and would send back to them any of theirs who came to him.

In short, wherever there is an explicit text, the believer has nothing but to obey Allah and His Messenger, as the Exalted says: “It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair” [al-Aḥzāb 33:36].
One should receive this with an open breast and contentment, for faith in what Allah and His Messenger have legislated, contentment with it and submission to it are obligatory, as the Exalted says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what is disputed between them, and then find within themselves no constraint over what you have decided, and submit in full submission” [al-Nisāʾ 4:65].

But where there is no explicit text from Allah and His Messenger, nor from any of the Companions and the Salaf of the nation whose word is followed, and something of the matter troubles the believer whose heart is at rest in faith and whose breast is opened by the light of knowledge and certainty, scratching at his breast because of a doubt that really exists,

and he finds no one to give him a ruling allowing it except someone who speaks from his own opinion, and who is not trusted in his knowledge and his religion but is known for following his desires, then the believer turns back to what scratches at his breast, even if these people give him a ruling.
Imam Aḥmad stated as much explicitly. Al-Marwazī said in Kitāb al-Waraʿ: I said to Abū ʿAbdillāh:
The Qaṭīʿah is easier for me than the other markets, but something about it has troubled my heart. He said: Its affair is a dirty, tainted affair. I said: So you dislike working in it?
He said: Leave that alone, if nothing troubles your heart. I said: Something about it has troubled my heart. He said: Ibn Masʿūd said: Sin is what pricks the hearts.
I said: Is this only by way of advice?
He said: What is it that troubles your heart?
I said: My heart has become agitated about it. He said: Sin is what pricks the hearts.

Something relating to the interpretation of the hadiths mentioned here has already been given in the explanation of the hadith of al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, “The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear”; in the explanation of the hadith of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī,
“Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt”; and in the explanation of the hadith, “If you feel no shame, do as you wish.”
The printed text reads «الحسين بن علي»; read «الحسن بن علي», as in the Arnaʾūṭ and Abū al-Nūr editions. Hadith 11, “Leave what makes you doubt”, is narrated by al-Ḥasan.
Groups of Shāfiʿī and Ḥanafī jurists who wrote on legal theory have discussed the question of inspiration (ilhām): is it a proof or not?

They mention a difference of opinion among themselves on it. A group of the scholars of our [Ḥanbalī] school stated that unveiling (kashf) is not a way of establishing rulings, and al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā took this from Aḥmad's words censuring those who speak about whisperings and passing thoughts.
Another group of the scholars of our school disagreed with them on this, and we have quoted Aḥmad's explicit statement here about turning back to what pricks the hearts.
Aḥmad and others censured those Sufis who spoke about whisperings and passing thoughts only because what they said about them rested on no evidence from the Sharīʿah,
but on mere opinion and taste (dhawq), just as he would reject speaking on questions of the lawful and the unlawful by mere opinion without evidence from the Sharīʿah.
As for turning back, in doubtful matters, to what pricks the hearts, the Prophetic texts and the legal verdicts of the Companions point to it; so how could Imam Aḥmad reject it after that,
especially when he has explicitly stated that one should turn back to it, in agreement with them?

The hadith has already been given: “Truthfulness is tranquillity, and lying is doubt.” So truthfulness is distinguished from lying by the heart's finding rest in it and recognising it, and by its recoiling from lying and rejecting it, as al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym said: Hadith has a light like the light of day, by which you recognise it, and a darkness like the darkness of night, by which you reject it.

Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of Rabīʿah, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Saʿīd ibn Suwayd, from Abū Ḥumayd and Abū Usayd, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “When you hear a hadith from me which your hearts recognise,

at which your hair and your skin soften, and which you see to be close to you, then I am the closest of you to it; and when you hear a hadith from me which your hearts reject, from which your hair and your skin recoil, and which you see to be far from you, then I am the farthest of you from it.”
It has been said that its chain meets Muslim's conditions,

because he recorded a hadith with this very chain. But this hadith is defective, for Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj reported it from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Saʿīd, from ʿAbbās ibn Sahl, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, as his own words; al-Bukhārī said: That is more correct.
Yaḥyā ibn Ādam reported, from Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, from Saʿīd al-Maqburī, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“When a hadith is related to you from me which you recognise and do not reject, believe it, for I say what is recognised and not rejected; and when a hadith is related to you from me which you reject and do not recognise, do not believe it,

for I do not say what is rejected and not recognised.” This hadith too is defective. Its chain has been reported from Ibn Abī Dhiʾb in differing ways, and the ḥuffāẓ reported it from him, from Saʿīd, in mursal form;

and the mursal version is the more correct according to the leading ḥuffāẓ, among them Ibn Maʿīn, al-Bukhārī, Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī and Ibn Khuzaymah, who said: I have not seen any of the scholars of hadith affirm it as connected.

Hadiths such as these, supposing them to be authentic, can only be understood to refer to the recognition possessed by the expert critics among the imams of hadith: those whose practice has been long with the speech of the Prophet ﷺ

and the speech of others, and with the condition of the narrators of hadiths and the transmitters of reports, and whose knowledge of their truthfulness and lying, their memory and their precision, is extensive. These have a special discernment in hadith that they alone possess,

just as the skilled money-changer alone knows coins, good and bad, pure and alloyed, and the skilled jeweller knows gems by assaying them. None of these can put into words the reason for his judgement,
or establish proof of it for anyone else. The sign of this is that a single hadith is put to a number of those who know this science, and they agree on the answer about it without any collusion.
This was put to the test among them more than once in the time of Abū Zurʿah and Abū Ḥātim, and it was found to be so, and the questioner said: I bear witness that this knowledge is inspiration.
Al-Aʿmash said: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī was a money-changer in hadith. I used to hear from men and then put what I had heard to him.
ʿAmr ibn Qays said: The hadith scholar should be like the money-changer who assays dirhams; for among dirhams there are counterfeit and debased ones, and so it is with hadith.
Al-Awzāʿī said: We used to hear a hadith and put it to our companions as one puts a counterfeit dirham to the money-changers: what they recognised we took, and what they rejected we left.
It was said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī: You say of something, “This is authentic,” and “This is not established.” On whose authority do you say that?

He said: Tell me, if you went to the assayer and showed him your dirhams, and he said, “This one is good and this one is debased,” would you ask him on whose authority he said so, or would you leave the matter to him?
He said: No, I would leave the matter to him. He said: This is the same; it comes from long sitting with it, debating it and experience of it.
Something similar is narrated from Imam Aḥmad too: he was asked, Abū ʿAbdillāh, you say, “This hadith is munkar”; how do you know, when you have not written down all hadith?
He said: We are like an assayer of gold coins (ʿayn) who has not had all the gold in his hands; yet when a dīnār comes into his hand he knows that it is good, or that it is bad.
Ibn Mahdī said: Knowing hadith is inspiration.
He also said: Our rejecting a hadith is, in the eyes of the ignorant, soothsaying.

Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī said: Knowing hadith is like a gemstone worth a hundred dīnārs and another like it in colour worth ten dirhams. He said: And just as the assayer cannot explain the reason for his judgement,
so we have been given a knowledge such that we cannot explain how we know that this hadith is a lie and that this hadith is munkar, except by what we recognise. He said:

The quality of a dīnār is known by comparing it with others: if it falls short in redness and purity, it is known to be adulterated. The kind of a gem is known by comparing it with others: if it differs in lustre and hardness,

it is known to be glass. The authenticity of a hadith is known by the integrity of its transmitters and by its being speech of a kind that could be the speech of prophethood; and its weakness and munkar status are known by its being narrated by a lone narrator whose integrity has not been established. And Allah knows best.

In any case, the expert critics who know the hidden defects (ʿilal) of hadith are very few individuals among the people of hadith. The first to become famous for speaking on the criticism of hadith was Ibn Sīrīn. He was succeeded by Ayyūb

al-Sakhtiyānī, from whom Shuʿbah took it; Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān and Ibn Mahdī took it from Shuʿbah; Aḥmad, ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and Ibn Maʿīn took it from those two; and the likes of al-Bukhārī, Abū Dāwūd, Abū Zurʿah and Abū Ḥātim took it from them.

The printed text places «وابنُ مهدي» after «أيوبُ» (“then Ayyūb and Ibn Mahdī succeeded him”), which breaks the chronology and leaves the dual «عنهما» without its second member. Read it after «يحيى القطان», as in the Arnaʾūṭ and Abū al-Nūr editions.
Abū Zurʿah used to say in his time: Few understand this. How rare it is! Once you go beyond one or two, how few you find who are good at this!
When Abū Zurʿah died, Abū Ḥātim said: The one who was good at this has gone — meaning Abū Zurʿah. There is not one left in Egypt or in Iraq who is good at this.
After Abū Zurʿah's death he was asked: Do you know anyone today who knows this? He said: No.
After these came a group, among them al-Nasāʾī, al-ʿUqaylī, Ibn ʿAdī and al-Dāraquṭnī.

Few who came after them have excelled in knowing this, so much so that Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī said at the beginning of his book al-Mawḍūʿāt (“The Fabricated Reports”): Those who understand this have become few; indeed, they are gone. And Allah knows best.
